observations: A large golden-yellow eye with a broad white highlight dominates the right half of the face; a much smaller, rounder dark eye sits to the left, creating a strongly mismatched pair against a flat pink ground.
The lower jaw is detached from the upper face mass, floating below a row of uneven cream and yellow teeth; a second row of smaller coiled forms sits further down, isolated on the pink ground.
Dense black hatching and short spiky marks radiate from the right edge and crown, mixing with scattered strokes of red, blue, and yellow against the otherwise muted olive-brown face mass.
reading: One eye swells to fill nearly a quarter of the image while its partner shrinks to a small dark circle — the face reads as off-balance before anything else registers. The detached lower jaw, drifting free with its own row of coiled forms below, adds a sense of things coming apart rather than holding together. The flat pink ground keeps the mood somewhere between unsettling and absurd.
contextAngle: Within the owned nifty-faces subset, this work sits between title neighbors nnxyz nifty faces #127 and nnxyz nifty faces #129. Where #127 fills its frame with dense multicolor scribble on orange and #129 settles into a quiet teal field, #128 uses a flat pink ground.

connections.reason: Both works use mismatched eye shapes and exposed teeth as main structural elements, but #127 scatters color across the whole surface while #128 concentrates color in the large eye and leaves the face mass in muted olive-brown.
Both works share a flat pink ground, and both place tight circular line work at a focal point — the spiral glasses in nnotb #169 and the large rounded eye here — against looser surrounding marks.

lookingQuestion: What does the gap between the upper and lower jaw — and the second floating row of forms below it — do to how you read the rest of the face?
ambiguities: The coiled forms below the main jaw could be a second jaw, a separate object, or purely abstract marks; the image does not resolve this.
The nnotb #169 pink-ground connection crosses collections and rests on a shared ground color and one formal echo; the link is suggestive rather than strong.
